title: Emergent Social Conventions and Collective Bias in LLM Populations
publisher: arXiv preprint (published in Science Advances 11(20), eadu9368, 2025); Ashery, Aiello, Baronchelli

key_points.claim: Universal social conventions emerge spontaneously in decentralized LLM-agent populations via a naming game with only local incentives (norm emergence).
key_points.evidence_quote: spontaneous emergence of universally adopted social conventions in decentralized populations of Large Language Model (LLM) agents

key_points.claim: Setup: random pairwise interactions, name pool W=10, memory H=5, N=24. Agents are rewarded for matching and penalized for mismatching. Four LLMs were tested (Llama-2-70b-Chat, Llama-3-70B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, Claude-3.5-Sonnet).
key_points.evidence_quote: we set the name pool size to W = 10 and the individual memory length to H = 5 for populations of N = 24 agents

key_points.claim: Convergence is a disorder-to-order transition with symmetry breaking. It happens by about round 15 for all models except Llama-2. It is robust for populations up to N=200 and pools up to W=26, and the classic naming-game model captures the dynamics.
key_points.evidence_quote: a shared social convention is established by population round 15 in all cases, except for Llama-2-70b-Chat

key_points.claim: Collective bias emerges even when individual agents are unbiased. It arises from the interaction dynamics and the diversity of agents' memory states.
key_points.evidence_quote: both social conventions and collective biases in the selection process emerge also in absence of individual biases

key_points.claim: Microscopic mechanism: agents almost always repeat a successful name and switch after a failure. An asymmetry between a 'strong' and a 'weak' convention appears by the third interaction.
key_points.evidence_quote: if an agent succeeds in the first interaction, it will almost surely continue to use the successful name in the next interaction (99.4%...). However, if an agent fails, it will almost surely switch names (97.3%

key_points.claim: Critical-mass dynamics: a committed minority of adversarial agents can overturn an established convention. The threshold depends on the convention's strength and on the LLM, ranging from 2% to 67%.
key_points.evidence_quote: committed groups as small as 2% (Llama-3-70B-Instruct) or as large as 67% (Llama-2-70b-Chat)

key_points.claim: Comparison with the human literature: theory predicts critical masses of 10–40%, and human experiments found about 25%. The authors deliberately use a minimal complex-systems design rather than high-fidelity human simulation, and they do not treat LLMs as proxies for humans.
key_points.evidence_quote: Empirical evidence from controlled social coordination experiments, which closely follow the scheme described above, supports a 25% threshold

key_points.claim: Once a convention has emerged it is a stable steady state. The strong convention has a larger and deeper basin of attraction.
key_points.evidence_quote: the basin of attraction of the strong convention is both larger and deeper than that of the weaker convention

reliability_notes: Full text was fetched; I read roughly the first 60% (intro, results, start of discussion). It is a peer-reviewed paper (Science Advances) with a preprint version. The experiments are simple: a naming game with small populations, one task type, and a few LLMs. The results may not generalize to richer LLM-agent societies.
